line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Bc5 Bc4 d6 O-O Bg4 d3 Nc6
teaches: The best developing move is the one that arrives carrying a threat — a knight that comes out eyeing the central jump forces your opponent to spend their next move on your plans instead of their own.
explains: The knight develops to c6 and takes the d4 square in hand, and with the bishop already pinning the defender on f3, the jump into d4 is a real threat the opponent has to answer at once. The developing move set the agenda.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Bc5 Bc4 d6 O-O Bg4 d3 Nc6 Be3 Bb6 h3 Bh5 Kh2 O-O Qd2 Bxf3 gxf3 Nh5
teaches: When the pawn cover in front of their king has been damaged, do not wait — get the wheels turning on that wing before they reorganise. A knight hopping toward the weakened squares stakes the claim, and every piece that follows finds the squares already prepared.
explains: The knight swings to h5 and takes both f4 and g3 in hand — the two dark squares the doubled pawns no longer guard. The factory starts running on the side of the board where the opponent's king lives, one hop ahead of their regrouping.

teaches: Two passed pawns on opposite sides of the board beat a lone king even when neither pawn has support — the king cannot stand in two doorways at once. Count the squares before agreeing to any trade that leaves this race: if the pawns are far enough apart, the position that looks thin is simply winning.
explains: One passed pawn stands on d3 and another on h3, a whole board apart, and the enemy king on one side cannot reach the other in time. The plan is the pawns' own legs — each step by one forces the king to abandon the other.
structural: two distant passers against a king judged by counting, not hope — the king cannot hold both doorways
